definition.text: Firewood is any wood used for fuel, usually as recognizable logs or branches rather than processed products such as pellets.

facts.text: Firewood is a renewable resource, but local demand can quickly outrun how fast trees regrow.
For most of human history firewood was the main fuel, and the right to gather it was a valued part of many medieval leases.
Along with clearing land for farming, gathering firewood is a cause of deforestation, and its smoke causes breathing problems.
Moving firewood long distances can spread tree pests, diseases and invasive species.

definition.text: Food security means having reliable access to enough affordable, healthy food.

facts.text: The 1996 World Food Summit defined it as all people at all times having physical and economic access to enough safe, nutritious food for an active, healthy life.
Close to 12% of the world's people, 928 million, were severely food insecure in 2020, 148 million more than in 2019.
Hunger is often caused not by a lack of food but by people being unable to reach the food that exists, usually because of poverty.
Intensive farming can trap land in a cycle of falling soil fertility and falling yields; deforestation and overgrazing also degrade land.
Overfishing poses serious risks to food security.
Losing crop diversity threatens food security because people rely on fewer and fewer varieties of fewer crop species.
Pollinator decline could endanger food security as well as unbalance ecosystems.

definition.text: Food security is usually broken into pillars: whether food is available, whether people can get it, how well they use it, and whether this stays stable over time.

facts.text: Availability is the supply of food through production, distribution and exchange.
Access covers whether food is affordable and how it is shared out, along with people's preferences.
Stability is the ability to get food over time; food insecurity can be passing, seasonal or chronic.
Sustainability, a further pillar, asks that food systems feed people now without undermining the bases for feeding future generations.
